retrieved.title: Papyrus in Ancient Egypt
retrieved.organization: The Metropolitan Museum of Art; Janice Kamrin
retrieved.text: In ancient Egypt, papyrus served as a writing material and as a resource for everyday objects. To make a writing surface, workers arranged strips from the stalk's inner pith in layers and dried them under pressure. Sheets could be joined into rolls. Egypt's dry conditions helped preserve papyrus documents. Surviving examples include letters, contracts, administrative records and religious texts. Most text used black ink, while red could emphasize particular material. Papyrus is a material; it is not the name of a writing system.

retrieved.text: Mesopotamia was centered in what is now Iraq. In southern Mesopotamia, urban institutions developed around 3400-3000 BCE. Cities combined monumental buildings with officials who organized economic, agricultural and religious activity. Uruk was an important early Sumerian city. Intensive irrigation agriculture supported city growth, and major temple estates directed canal maintenance. Early writing appeared in southern Mesopotamia around 3400 BCE.
